# Stationary volume and section marginals admit neither universal convex-order direction

The jointly concave cap-root quantile lift retains substantial compatibility, but it does **not** impose either universal convex-order direction between the normalized fiber volumes and the normalized stationary section measures. The following two exact actual convex bodies demonstrate opposite strict directions. Both have three positive fibers, all three cuts are proper, their true mixed centroid is `(0,0,0)`, and the tested cap is active at an actual global depth maximizer. This is an obstruction to the stated auxiliary comparisons, not to OC or to comparisons with additional defect terms.

## 1. A common exact planar profile

Let

\[
D=\{(x,y):|x|+|y|\le1\},\qquad |D|=2.
\]

For its vertical functional `L(x,y)=y`, the tail area is

\[
F(s)=\begin{cases}
(1-s)^2,&0\le s\le1,\\
2-(1+s)^2,&-1\le s\le0.
\end{cases}
\]

The inverse square-root-tail quantile, meaning `F(U_0(t))=t^2`, is

\[
U_0(t)=\begin{cases}
1-t,&0\le t\le1,\\
-1+\sqrt{2-t^2},&1\le t\le\sqrt2.
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

This is decreasing and concave, with matching derivative `-1` at `t=1`. Its perspective

\[
V(R,t)=R U_0(t/R)
=\begin{cases}
R-t,&t\le R,\\
-R+\sqrt{2R^2-t^2},&R\le t\le\sqrt2R
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
\]

is jointly concave on `R>0,0<=t<=sqrt(2)R`. It is nondecreasing in `R` on this domain: the first branch has derivative one, and the second has derivative `-1+2R/sqrt(2R^2-t^2)>=1`. Thus replacing `R` by a positive concave function of the real base preserves joint concavity in that base and `t`.

For a fiber `R D+(0,s)`, the cap-root quantile is exactly `s+V(R,t)`. At a proper cut `U(z,c_z)=0`, define `beta_z=-partial_t U(z,c_z)>0`. Its horizontal section length is

\[
a_z=\frac{2c_z}{\beta_z}.
\tag{3}
\]

The three-dimensional mixed ambient coordinates below are `(z,x,y)`, with integer base `z`. The cap under test is the full ambient halfspace `H={y>=0}`.

## 2. The volume marginal can be less dispersed than the section marginal

For `-1<=z<=1` put `R(z)=2-|z|` and take

\[
C_A=\{(z,x,y):-1\le z\le1,\quad |x|+|y|\le R(z)\}.
\]

It is a compact convex body. Its actual integer fibers have radii `(1,2,1)`. The quantile lift is `U_A(z,t)=V(R(z),t)`, jointly concave by (2), on its actual convex domain.

At indices `(-1,0,1)`, the quantities are

\[
w=(2,8,2),\qquad r=\sqrt w=(\sqrt2,2\sqrt2,\sqrt2),
\]
\[
c=(1,2,1),\qquad\beta=(1,1,1),\qquad a=(2,4,2).
\]

Thus both the volume and section distributions have integer mean zero, but

\[
\mathbb E_{w/\sum w}[z^2]=\frac13
<\frac12=\mathbb E_{a/\sum a}[z^2].
\tag{4}
\]

In particular, the volume distribution does **not** dominate the section distribution in convex order. There are no zero section weights or captured endpoint fibers, and even all the inverse-quantile derivatives `beta_z` are equal in this example.

## 3. The volume marginal can be more dispersed than the section marginal

Now take the sheared product

\[
C_B=\{(z,x,y):-1\le z\le1,\quad |x|+|y-z/2|\le1\}.
\]

Its actual three integer fibers are `D+(0,z/2)`, and the exact quantile lift is

\[
U_B(z,t)=z/2+U_0(t),\qquad 0\le t\le\sqrt2.
\]

It is jointly concave. At the three indices the relevant quantities are

\[
w=(2,2,2),\qquad r=(\sqrt2,\sqrt2,\sqrt2),
\]
\[
c=(1/2,1,\sqrt7/2),\qquad
\beta=(1,1,\sqrt7),\qquad a=(1,2,1).
\]

Again both normalized distributions have mean zero, whereas now

\[
\mathbb E_{w/\sum w}[z^2]=\frac23
>\frac12=\mathbb E_{a/\sum a}[z^2].
\tag{5}
\]

Thus the section distribution does **not** dominate the volume distribution in convex order. Both examples have exactly the same proper-section index support.

## 4. Actual global optimality, stationarity, and closed halfspaces

Both bodies are centrally symmetric under `(z,x,y)->(-z,-x,-y)`, as are their actual mixed measures. Hence their true mixed centroids are the origin, a point of the middle fiber. Every closed halfspace through the origin has mass at least half the total: its reflected halfspace has the same mass, their union covers the support, and any boundary mass is counted in both. This argument includes vertical halfspaces with positive boundary-fiber mass.

Every nonvertical horizontal cap through the origin has exactly half the mass, because its boundary has zero planar measure on every fiber. Thus `H={y>=0}` and its opposite are equal-budget active caps at the origin. For any other candidate point, a horizontal halfspace in the direction away from the origin, through that point, has mass at most half the total, by symmetry of the `y` distribution. Therefore the maximum mixed depth is exactly `1/2` and is attained at the origin in each example.

The full section of either body by `y=0` is itself centrally symmetric, so its coarea centroid is also the origin. In particular `sum z a_z=0`, the continuous section first moments vanish, and the opposite active normals balance with equal weights, including their equal coarea factors. All cuts displayed above are proper with finite positive `beta_z`; equation (1) is continuously differentiable at its joining point. The moment identity

\[
\int_{K_z} y\,dx\,dy=2\int_0^{r_z}t U(z,t)\,dt
\]

holds by the exact inverse-tail formula; its two sides vanish separately in the first family and equal `z` in the second family. Summing gives the actual continuous centroid equation in either case.

Consequently joint quantile concavity, actual volume centering, actual full-section centering, proper cuts, and actual active global-center status all coexist with either strict variance order (4)--(5). A possible higher-dimensional extension must use something beyond a fixed universal convex-order relation between these two marginals. The example does not impose a below-OC budget or minimizing-body hypothesis.

## 5. The two natural Jensen heights also have no fixed order

Joint concavity permits two centered applications of Jensen. The volume-coordinate law has conditional density `d t^(d-1)/r_z^d` on `0<=t<=r_z`, and the actual centroid equation makes its mean quantile value zero. Its mean height is

\[
B_{\rm vol}=\frac d{d+1}\frac{\sum_z r_z^{d+1}}{\sum_z r_z^d},
\]

so Jensen gives `U(0,B_vol)>=0`. The stationary section law on the points `(z,c_z)`, with weights proportional to `a_z`, has mean base zero and quantile value zero at each point. Its mean height is

\[
B_{\rm sec}=\frac{\sum_z a_z c_z}{\sum_z a_z},
\]

and Jensen likewise gives `U(0,B_sec)>=0`. In the two examples, both heights are thus at most the central cap root `c_0`, but their mutual order reverses:

\[
C_A:\quad B_{\rm vol}=\frac{10\sqrt2}{9}>\frac32=B_{\rm sec};
\]
\[
C_B:\quad B_{\rm vol}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}
<\frac{5+\sqrt7}{8}=B_{\rm sec}.
\]

The first strict inequality is equivalent to `800>729` after squaring positive sides. The second reduces, after two legitimate positive-side squarings, to `56700>50176`. Thus neither order between these two scalar Jensen heights follows from the full stated geometry and stationarity either.

## 6. A single actual system with convex-order incomparable marginals

One can strengthen the obstruction: the two marginals need not be comparable in **either** direction even after inspecting the particular body. On the indices `-2,-1,0,1,2`, take diamond radii and vertical shifts

\[
R=(1/10,1,1,1,1/10),\qquad
h=(0,-9/20,0,9/20,0).
\]

Extend `A=R+h` and `B=R-h` by adjacent affine interpolation. Their values are

\[
A=(1/10,11/20,1,29/20,1/10),
\quad B=(1/10,29/20,1,11/20,1/10).
\]

Both sequences are concave: the slopes of `A` are `(9/20,9/20,9/20,-27/20)`, and those of `B` are their reversed negatives. Therefore

\[
C=\{(z,x,y):-2\le z\le2,\quad
|x|+y\le A(z),\quad |x|-y\le B(z)\}
\]

is a compact convex body whose actual integer fibers are exactly `R_zD+(0,h_z)`.

The quantile lift is again `h(z)+V(R(z),t)`. Joint concavity can be checked directly, rather than assumed from a slice theorem: the function

\[
(A,B,t)\longmapsto (A-B)/2+V((A+B)/2,t)
\]

is concave and nondecreasing in both `A` and `B`. This follows from concavity of `V` and `V_R>=1` in (2). Composition with the two concave functions `A(z),B(z)` proves joint concavity on the actual domain.

All five horizontal cuts are proper. Their masses and section lengths are

\[
w=(1/50,2,2,2,1/50),\quad M=151/25,
\]
\[
a=(1/5,11/10,2,11/10,1/5),\quad \sum a=23/5.
\]

For additional exact quantile data,

\[
c=(1/10,11/20,1,\sqrt{679}/20,1/10),
\quad\beta=(1,1,1,\sqrt{679}/11,1),
\]

and `a_z=2c_z/beta_z` as required. Central symmetry gives all the actual centroid, global depth, active-cap, and section-stationarity conclusions of §4.

Consider the two convex test functions `f(z)=|z|` and `g(z)=(|z|-1)_+`. The exact normalized expectations are

\[
\mathbb E_w f=102/151,\qquad \mathbb E_a f=15/23,
\qquad \mathbb E_w f-\mathbb E_a f=81/3473>0,
\]
\[
\mathbb E_w g=1/151,\qquad \mathbb E_a g=2/23,
\qquad \mathbb E_w g-\mathbb E_a g=-279/3473<0.
\]

Thus neither centered probability law dominates the other in convex order. In particular, the signed normalized difference has four sign changes across its common proper-section support, with pattern `(-,+,-,+,-)`. A replacement for the interval proof's one-chord comparison cannot assume either an adaptable convex-order direction or at most two sign changes under the present quantile and stationarity hypotheses alone.
